questions.prompt: Which statement about infectious disease worldwide vs the US matches the lecture?

options.text: It's fourth worldwide but the leading cause of death in the US
It is rarely a cause of death anywhere in the world today
It's the leading cause of death worldwide but fourth in the US
It's the leading cause of death both worldwide and in the US

questions.explanation: Heart disease, cancer, and stroke rank higher in the US.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows microbial antagonism by changing the environment?

options.text: S. epidermidis crowds S. aureus off the skin
E. coli secretes bacteriocins against Salmonella
Lactobacillus lowers vaginal pH, inhibiting Candida
A fecal transplant replaces lost gut flora

questions.explanation: The other two mechanisms are outcompeting and bacteriocins.

questions.prompt: Which statement about signs and symptoms is FALSE?

options.text: Symptoms are felt by the patient.

questions.explanation: Malaise is a symptom — only the patient feels it.

questions.prompt: A patient's bloodstream is full of bacteria and she develops septic shock. Which pair of terms applies?
questions.explanation: Bacteria in blood + extreme immune reaction.

questions.prompt: Describe the five stages of infectious disease in terms of microbe numbers and signs/symptoms.
questions.explanation: Incubation: microbes rising slowly, no signs/symptoms. Prodromal: rising numbers, mild signs/symptoms. Period of illness: exponential growth, most severe signs/symptoms (death possible at the peak). Decline: numbers fall as immunity or drugs work; symptoms subside. Convalescence: no symptoms, but microbes not yet gone.

questions.prompt: Explain why females are at greater risk of E. coli UTIs and what simple habit helps.
questions.explanation: In females, the anus is very close to the urethral opening and the urethra is short, so E. coli from the colon reaches the bladder easily. Wiping front to back keeps bacteria moving away from the urethra. (Female sex is a predisposing factor.)

questions.prompt: Which is an infectious but non-communicable disease?
questions.explanation: Slides also list Lyme disease.

questions.prompt: Which statement about herd immunity is correct?

options.text: Unvaccinated people are protected when most others are immune
It works only for bacterial diseases, never for viral ones
It only protects the people who actually received the vaccine
It requires every person to have caught the disease once

questions.explanation: Measles is the lecture's cautionary example.

questions.prompt: A coworker's cough reaches you at 2 meters. Why isn't this called droplet transmission?

options.text: Droplet is under 1 meter; farther than that is airborne
Droplets must first land on a fomite to count as droplet
Droplets only come from sneezes, never from coughs
Coughs are always counted as direct contact transmission

questions.explanation: Distance defines the category.

questions.prompt: Which statement about HAIs is FALSE?

options.text: HAIs occur only in hospitals, not clinics or nursing homes.
UTIs are the most common HAI.
Hand washing is the most effective prevention.
They were formerly called nosocomial infections.

questions.explanation: Any healthcare facility counts.

questions.prompt: Which virulence factor works by hiding the pathogen inside host cells?
questions.explanation: Salmonella typhimurium.

questions.prompt: Which pathogen product causes host damage by stealing a nutrient rather than by toxins or lysis?
questions.explanation: Iron is pulled from red blood cells and enzymes.

questions.prompt: List and explain the three portals of entry, noting which is most common and why.
questions.explanation: Broken skin (intact skin is a strong barrier); mucous membranes — the most common, because they line surfaces that exchange materials with the outside (respiratory, digestive tracts); parenteral route — something plunges through intact skin (needle, nail, bite).

questions.prompt: Contrast exotoxins and endotoxins: source, chemistry, release, and one example each.
questions.explanation: Exotoxins are proteins secreted mostly by Gram-positive bacteria (often prophage genes): e.g., botulinum A-B toxin. Endotoxins are part of the Gram-negative cell wall (LPS), released when the cell dies, causing excessive immune responses.

questions.prompt: Which virulence factor and organism pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: M-protein adheres and blocks phagocytosis.

questions.prompt: A tick-borne bacterium multiplies in the tick before infecting humans; the tick picked it up from deer. Identify the reservoir and vector type.

options.text: Humans are the reservoir; the tick is a fomite
Deer are the reservoir; the tick is a biological vector
Deer are a vehicle; the tick is a mechanical vector
The tick is the reservoir; deer are a mechanical vector

questions.explanation: The pathogen reproduces in the tick.

questions.prompt: Which statement about first-line defenses is FALSE?

options.text: Sweat leaves salt behind when it dries.
Tears flush the eye and contain lysozyme.
Urine is the most acidic first-line fluid.
Earwax contains sebum and is acidic.

questions.explanation: Gastric juice (pH ~2) is the most acidic; urine is about 6.

questions.prompt: Why do nasal mucus and tears eventually reach the stomach?

options.text: They are absorbed into the blood and filtered out by the stomach
Mast cells carry them to the stomach after releasing histamine
Macrophages carry them to the stomach through the lymph vessels
Tears drain to the nose, cilia move mucus up, and both get swallowed

questions.explanation: Stomach acid destroys the trapped microbes.

questions.prompt: Which cell is known as a 'mall cop' that sounds the alarm?
questions.explanation: It holds histamine vesicles.

questions.prompt: Which sign of inflammation is caused by swelling pressing on tissue?
questions.explanation: Swelling comes from leaky vessels.

questions.prompt: Describe what pus is and how an abscess forms and heals.
questions.explanation: Pus = dead neutrophils, phagocytic waste, and tissue fluid. Clotting walls the infection in, forming an abscess; macrophages engulf the pus and debris, the area scabs over and heals — large sites may scar.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between innate and adaptive immunity using fever and antibodies as examples.
questions.explanation: Innate (nonspecific) defenses like fever are present at birth, don't target a specific antigen, and don't improve with exposure. Adaptive (specific) defenses like antibodies develop over life, target one antigen, and improve with repeated exposure (memory).

questions.prompt: Which feature makes the ciliary escalator part of the FIRST line rather than the second?

options.text: It releases histamine to start the inflammatory response
It recognizes specific antigens on the trapped microbes
It physically removes microbes before they invade tissue
It uses white blood cells to eat trapped microbes

questions.explanation: First-line = barriers and surface chemicals.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a phagolysosome's enzymes?
questions.explanation: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes.

questions.prompt: Which statement about cytokines is FALSE?

options.text: Interferon is a pyrogen that resets the hypothalamus.
Cytokines are small proteins that regulate immune responses.

questions.explanation: Pyrogens are interleukins; interferon is antiviral.

questions.prompt: Which trigger would activate complement in the SPECIFIC way?

options.text: Antibodies bound side by side on a bacterium
A cut that damages mast cells

questions.explanation: Antibodies make the activation specific.

questions.prompt: Which explains why interferon doesn't save the cell that makes it?

options.text: Interferon is toxic to the very cell that produces and secretes it
The virus is already replicating inside it by the time it makes interferon
The infected cell has no interferon receptors on its surface
Interferon only works against bacteria, not against viruses

questions.explanation: It warns neighbors instead.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes how complement causes inflammation?

options.text: Interferon binds mast cells and releases histamine
C3b coats mast cells so macrophages can eat them
C3a and C5a bind mast cells, which release histamine
C9 punches pores in mast cells, spilling histamine

questions.explanation: Same outcome as tissue damage, different trigger.

questions.prompt: Describe opsonization by complement and explain the word's meaning.
questions.explanation: Activated C3 splits; C3b coats the bacterium, and the macrophage's C3b receptors grab it, enhancing phagocytosis. 'Opsonize' means to cater or prepare for eating.

questions.prompt: Explain how interferon protects a tissue from viral spread and why it causes side effects as a drug.
questions.explanation: An infected cell secretes interferon; it binds neighbors' receptors so they make antiviral proteins that destroy viral RNA. As a drug, injected interferon spreads everywhere and AVPs destroy cells' own RNA, causing significant side effects.

questions.prompt: Which defense, if missing, would most directly allow Gram-negative bacteria in the blood to avoid being burst?
questions.explanation: MAC causes cytolysis.

questions.prompt: Mannose and LPS both trigger complement nonspecifically because they are:

options.text: Antibodies made by activated B cells
Common molecules shared by many microbes
Human self-markers on healthy body cells
Viral RNA molecules inside infected cells

questions.explanation: Broad recognition.

questions.prompt: Which statement about antibody mechanisms is FALSE?

options.text: IgG triggers mast cells to release histamine.

questions.explanation: Only IgE triggers mast cells.

questions.prompt: Which antibody class is the first made and also serves as the B cell receptor (as a monomer)?
questions.explanation: Secreted as a pentamer.

questions.prompt: Why does a breastfed infant get protection against gut pathogens?

options.text: IgA in breast milk neutralizes pathogens in the gut (natural passive immunity)
IgG in breast milk crosses the gut into the blood and creates memory
Breast milk raises gut pH to 9

questions.explanation: IgA works mainly by neutralization.

questions.prompt: Which change would make a B cell's antibodies bind a DIFFERENT antigen?
questions.explanation: Variable regions form the binding site.

questions.prompt: Compare plasma cells and memory B cells.
questions.explanation: Both come from a selected B cell's clonal expansion. Plasma cells secrete large amounts of antibody now and lack B cell receptors. Memory B cells keep receptors, don't secrete antibodies yet, and stay in circulation for a faster, stronger secondary response.

questions.prompt: Explain why the secondary immune response usually prevents illness, referring to the titer graph.
questions.explanation: Memory cells mean no week-long search for the matching B cell; plasma cells form quickly, so IgG rises sooner, much higher, and stays high longer — clearing the pathogen before disease develops.

questions.prompt: Which antibody mechanism would best help against a large parasitic worm?
questions.explanation: Too big to eat; it must be destroyed by released chemicals.

questions.prompt: Which describes humoral immunity?

options.text: T cell killing of virus-infected cells
Barrier defenses of the skin and mucus

questions.explanation: Named after the bodily humors.

questions.prompt: Why can some B cells be activated without helper T cells?

options.text: They use CD8 to bind antigen on MHC-1 directly
They are already plasma cells that need no signal
A repeating antigen binds many receptors at once
They are activated by interferon from nearby cells

questions.explanation: T-independent activation.

questions.prompt: Which statement about apoptosis is FALSE?

options.text: It can be induced by granzyme.
It spills contents that cause strong inflammation.

questions.explanation: Macrophages clean up first, avoiding inflammation.

questions.prompt: Which pair of cells can each kill target cells using perforin and granzymes?

options.text: Helper T cells and plasma cells
Cytotoxic T cells and NK cells

questions.explanation: Both are killer lymphocytes.

questions.prompt: A tumor cell keeps MHC-1 but displays a mutated protein on it. Which cell is best suited to destroy it?
questions.explanation: Foreign antigen on MHC-1 → CD8 T cell. NK cells target cells LACKING MHC-1.

questions.prompt: Explain T-dependent B cell activation in order, naming the cells, display proteins, and signals.
questions.explanation: Phagocyte (APC) engulfs pathogen, displays antigen on MHC-2 → helper T cell binds (TCR + CD4) → APC's interleukin activates and clones it → helper T secretes interleukin to attract B cells → matching B cell binds antigen and displays it on MHC-2 → helper T binds and secretes interleukin → B cell activated → plasma and memory cells.

questions.prompt: Explain why the CD4/MHC-2 and CD8/MHC-1 pairing protects immune cells and how its failure relates to disease.
questions.explanation: Immune cells display antigens on MHC-2, which only CD4 helper T cells can bind; CD8 cytotoxic T cells can only bind MHC-1, so they can't kill antigen-presenting immune cells. When this recognition system fails, autoimmune diseases can result.

questions.prompt: What does a high WBC count usually suggest, and what can a low count suggest?

options.text: High: anemia from too few red cells; low: infection only
High: infection; low: AIDS, autoimmune disease, or drugs
High: dehydration; low: an unusually healthy immune system
High: seasonal allergies only; low: a recent vaccination

questions.explanation: Per the lecture.

questions.prompt: In the rapid antigen strip, why are the test-line antibodies fixed to the strip?

options.text: So they neutralize the red dye before it reaches C
So they can bind the dyed chicken antibodies there
So they catch the dyed antibody–antigen complex in one spot
So they can travel up the strip along with the sample

questions.explanation: Fixed antibodies make the line.

questions.prompt: Which statement about COVID vaccines is FALSE?

options.text: DNA vaccines are transcribed into mRNA in the nucleus.
mRNA vaccines must enter the nucleus to work.
Both lead cells to make the spike protein.

questions.explanation: mRNA is translated in the cytoplasm; DNA must reach the nucleus.

questions.prompt: Which vaccine type targets a bacterial toxin rather than the bacterium itself?
questions.explanation: Tetanus, diphtheria.

questions.prompt: Why did Ehrlich try Salvarsan on syphilis after it worked on trypanosomes?

options.text: Both organisms are viruses with similar capsids
Spirochetes and trypanosomes looked alike to him
Both organisms cause African sleeping sickness
Both organisms make penicillin in culture

questions.explanation: He didn't realize one was a bacterium and the other a protozoan.

questions.prompt: Which antimicrobial is matched with a NON-bacterial target?
questions.explanation: Others: Flagyl (protozoa), Vermox (worms), Tamiflu (viruses).

questions.prompt: Describe three advantages of phage therapy over antibiotics and one requirement.
questions.explanation: Highly specific (spares normal flora), small dose that self-amplifies, and self-eliminating once the pathogen is gone. Requirement: you must identify the exact bacterial pathogen to choose the right phage.

questions.prompt: Explain quorum sensing using Vibrio fischeri and how Bassler's inhibitors might treat infections.
questions.explanation: Bacteria release a signal and have receptors for it; when enough are present, the signal binds neighbors and they act together — V. fischeri on the bobtail squid all bioluminesce at once. Pathogens use it to release toxins together. Inhibitors block the receptors so bacteria never sense a quorum and never turn toxic.

questions.prompt: Which vaccine is attenuated, per the slides?
questions.explanation: Salk is inactivated.

questions.prompt: Penicillin's discovery depended on noticing which phenomenon?

options.text: A zone of inhibition around a mold
Milkmaids who were immune to smallpox
A dye collecting in nerve endings
Bacteria glowing on a bobtail squid

questions.explanation: Fleming's contaminated staph plate.
